Page 3

Recall

Analytically find solutions to three types of “simple” systems.

Now, we can use substitution to turn any system of first-order ODEs into one of these simple forms.

Page 4

Recall: “Simple” Systems

NameSystemGeneral Solution
Uncoupled \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = ax\)
\(\dfrac{dy}{dt} = by\) 		\(x(t) = Ce^{at}\)
\(y(t) = De^{bt}\)
Partially Coupled \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = ax + y\)
\(\dfrac{dy}{dt} = ay\) 		\(x(t) = (Dt + C)e^{at}\)
\(y(t) = De^{at}\)
Complex Uncoupled \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = ax - by\)
\(\dfrac{dy}{dt} = bx + ay\) 		\(x(t) = (C_1\cos(bt) - C_2\sin(bt))e^{at}\)
\(y(t) = (C_1\sin(bt) + C_2\cos(bt))e^{at}\)
Handwritten annotation at bottom right references “Dynamic Behavior.”

Page 5

Recall: Vectors and Linear Combinations

Definition (Linear Combination): Given vectors \(\vec{e}_1\) and \(\vec{e}_2\), a linear combination is

\[ x\,\vec{e}_1 + y\,\vec{e}_2 \]

where \(x\) and \(y\) are scalar coefficients.

Using standard column-vector notation:

\[ x\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix} + y\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix} \]

Vector addition is performed entry-by-entry:

\[ \begin{bmatrix}a\\b\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}c\\d\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}a+c\\b+d\end{bmatrix} \]

Page 6

Matrices

Linear combinations are important. We introduce a shorthand using matrix multiplication.

The matrix-vector product computes a linear combination of the matrix’s columns:

\[ x\,\vec{v}_1 + y\,\vec{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} \mid & \mid \\ \vec{v}_1 & \vec{v}_2 \\ \mid & \mid \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix} \]

Key idea: Matrix-vector multiplication is shorthand for a linear combination of the columns of the matrix.

Page 7

Matrix Multiplication – Worked Example

Taking 2 units of the first column and 3 units of the second column:

Example:

\[ \begin{bmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2\\3\end{bmatrix} = 2\begin{bmatrix}a\\c\end{bmatrix} + 3\begin{bmatrix}b\\d\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}2a\\2c\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}3b\\3d\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}2a+3b\\2c+3d\end{bmatrix} \]

Page 8

Matrix Multiplication – Practice

You try:

Compute the following matrix-vector product:

\[ \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix} \]

Page 9

Matrix Multiplication as a Transformation

Matrix multiplication can be understood as a rule which inputs points in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) and outputs points in \(\mathbb{R}^2\).

Definition: Multiplication by a matrix with 2 rows and 2 columns defines a transformation (linear map) \(\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2\).

Page 10

Matrix Multiplication – Stretching

Consider what the following diagonal matrix does to points in the plane:

\[ \begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}2x\\3y\end{bmatrix} \]

This matrix stretches by a factor of 2 in the \(x\)-direction and by a factor of 3 in the \(y\)-direction.

The slide shows a grid of dots representing points in \(\mathbb{R}^2\). After multiplication by the diagonal matrix, the dots spread outward: horizontally by a factor of 2 and vertically by a factor of 3.

Page 11

Matrix Multiplication – Coordinate Convention

Convention: When plotting vectors as points in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), the first entry of the vector corresponds to the vertical axis, and the second entry corresponds to the horizontal axis (as used throughout this course).

The slide shows two diagrams with labeled axes illustrating that for a vector \(\begin{bmatrix}a\\b\end{bmatrix}\), the value \(a\) is plotted on the vertical axis and \(b\) on the horizontal axis.

Page 12

Matrix Multiplication – Stretch and Rotation

Matrices can encode both stretching and rotation simultaneously.

  • A diagonal matrix scales points outward (stretch).
  • Another matrix can rotate points about the origin.
  • A general matrix can combine both effects.
Two side-by-side diagrams show a set of points before and after two different transformations: the left diagram shows points spread outward (scaling), and the right diagram shows points rotated about the origin (rotation).

Page 13

Simple Systems – Transition to Linear Algebra Notation

Observe that if we define \(\vec{r} = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix}\), then the uncoupled system becomes:

\[ \vec{r}\,' = \begin{bmatrix} a & 0 \\ 0 & b \end{bmatrix} \vec{r} \]

and its general solution can be written in vector form:

\[ \vec{r}(t) = C\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}e^{at} + D\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}e^{bt} \]

This rewrites the scalar system as a matrix ODE \(\vec{r}\,' = A\vec{r}\), making the connection to linear algebra explicit.

Page 14

“Simple” Systems – Linear Algebra Version

Let the standard basis vectors be \(\vec{e}_1 = \begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}\) and \(\vec{e}_2 = \begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}\).

NameSystem (Matrix Form)General Solution
Uncoupled \(\vec{r}\,' = \begin{bmatrix} a & 0 \\ 0 & b \end{bmatrix}\vec{r}\) \(\vec{r}(t) = C\,\vec{e}_1\, e^{at} + D\,\vec{e}_2\, e^{bt}\)
Partially Coupled \(\vec{r}\,' = \begin{bmatrix} a & 1 \\ 0 & a \end{bmatrix}\vec{r}\) \(\vec{r}(t) = \bigl(C\,\vec{e}_1 + D(\vec{e}_1\,t + \vec{e}_2)\bigr)e^{at}\)
Complex Uncoupled \(\vec{r}\,' = \begin{bmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a \end{bmatrix}\vec{r}\) \(\vec{r}(t) = C_1\bigl(\cos(bt)\,\vec{e}_1 + \sin(bt)\,\vec{e}_2\bigr)e^{at} + C_2\bigl(-\sin(bt)\,\vec{e}_1 + \cos(bt)\,\vec{e}_2\bigr)e^{at}\)
